concept.name: Cash settlement
concept.definition: A method of settling futures, options, and other derivatives whereby the seller pays the buyer the cash value of the underlying, or a cash amount based on the level of an index or price, according to a procedure specified in the contract, instead of delivering the asset itself.
concept.intuition: Cash settlement settles the score in money only: at expiry the contract simply pays out the difference, so no barrels, shares, or bonds ever move.
concept.mechanics: At maturity, positions are valued against the final settlement price computed by the exchange's specified procedure (e.g., a special opening quotation of an index), and the clearing organization credits or debits the difference. Cash settlement is standard where the underlying is not practically deliverable, such as equity indexes.
concept.failure_modes: The settlement procedure itself becomes the point of fragility: if the reference price is derived from a short window or a manipulable market, the final settlement value can be distorted, and hedges calibrated to continuous prices can slip.
concept.misconceptions: Cash-settled does not mean 'synthetic' or less connected to the underlying — arbitrage against the cash market still enforces convergence to the settlement value; nor does it mean daily P&L differs, since all futures are marked to market daily regardless of final settlement style.
concept.example: At expiration, an E-mini S&P 500 futures position is settled in cash against the special opening quotation of the S&P 500 index; no shares of the 500 companies are delivered.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
